analysis.one_liner: Creates government-funded jobs at living wages, paid for with a small tax on stock and derivatives trades.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a hearing or vote: it was referred to two House committees in March 2012 and to a subcommittee in September, and neither ever acted before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a Full Employment Trust Fund that pays states, cities, and tribes to hire unemployed people for community work — repairing schools and parks, removing blight, staffing child care and Head Start, and feeding hungry families. The jobs would pay at least what similar public employees earn, last at least 12 months, and include benefits and child care support. The fund would be financed by a new tax on securities trades — 0.25% on stocks and 0.02% on futures, swaps, and credit default swaps — with retirement accounts and mutual funds exempt. If unemployment rose despite the program, the Federal Reserve would lend the fund extra money to keep hiring going.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed and underemployed workers get jobs at prevailing public-sector wages with benefits, a 12-month minimum commitment, and support services like child care. Distressed communities get repairs to schools, parks, and housing, blight removal, expanded child care and emergency food programs, and jobs for disadvantaged youth. At least 35% of jobs must go to people from severely disadvantaged groups.

how_it_helps.text: Creates jobs for certified unemployed individuals in construction, child care, education, blight removal, emergency food programs, and broadband projects, targeted to the areas with the worst unemployment, poverty, foreclosures, and poor health.
Guarantees funded workers at least 12 months of employment at 35-40 hours if they want full time, paid no less than comparable public-sector wages, with prevailing wages on construction work.

Requires at least 80% of each project's funds to go to wages, benefits, and support services such as child care, and bars employers from using funded workers to replace or displace existing employees.
Exempts retirement accounts (401(k)s, IRAs, 529s) and mutual fund investments from the trading tax, so ordinary savers' accounts are not taxed directly.

analysis.who_pays: Securities trading firms and exchanges pay a tax on every covered trade — 0.25% of the value for stocks, 0.02% for futures, swaps, and credit default swaps. Active traders, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms bear the largest costs; some of that cost can be passed to institutional investors, though retirement accounts and mutual funds are exempt.

drawbacks.text: The bill levies a tax on every covered stock trade (0.25%) and derivatives trade (0.02%) in U.S. markets or by U.S. persons, payable by trading facilities or purchasers, and requires withholding when the buyer is foreign.
A tax on each trade raises the cost of active trading and can push some trading to foreign venues, which would shrink the tax base that funds the jobs program (a known effect of transaction taxes).

The trust fund's size depends entirely on how much the trading tax raises each year, and the bill makes deposits subject to the availability of appropriations — so the jobs program's scale would be uncertain, with Federal Reserve loans kicking in only if unemployment rose more than one percentage point in a year.

Jobs are limited to people who register with the state employment service and meet specific unemployment criteria, and participants must stay registered, respond to job referrals, and accept suitable private jobs when offered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: At roughly 8% unemployment in 2012, a program that directly hires the jobless at prevailing wages in visibly useful community work would have put income into households that would spend it locally. The funding tax falls on high-volume traders rather than retirement savers, who are exempt, but it would make frequent trading more expensive and could push some activity offshore, weakening the revenue that sustains the jobs. The honest tradeoff is between a large, direct attack on joblessness and a new levy whose revenue and market effects are hard to predict.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees in March 2012 and to a subcommittee in September, neither ever held a hearing or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on March 28, 2012, and 61 House Democrats cosponsored it; no Republican did.
It was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
On September 26, 2012, part of it was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training — the last action ever recorded.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities traders and exchanges never paid the tax, and the unemployed workers the bill would have hired remained jobless. The committee chairs who held the bill avoided any recorded position on it.

for.name: 61 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Financial services industry
against.role: Securities exchanges, brokers, and high-frequency trading firms
against.what_they_did: Opposed securities transaction taxes of this kind, which would tax every trade they execute.

sides.party_line_note: All 61 cosponsors were Democrats with no Republican support on record, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-led committees that held it.

industries.industry: Securities and derivatives trading (exchanges, brokers, hedge funds, high-frequency traders)
industries.note: The bill taxes every covered stock trade at 0.25% and every futures, swap, or credit default swap trade at 0.02%, payable by trading facilities or purchasers. The revenue funds the jobs program, so the industry's cost is the program's funding — and retirement accounts and mutual funds are exempt, concentrating the levy on high-volume professional trading.

industries.industry: State and local governments, tribes, and community-based nonprofits
industries.note: They would receive grants to hire workers for schools, parks, housing, child care, and food programs, with at least 80% of project funds going to wages and benefits.
The bill requires that at least a quarter of the seats on state and local workforce investment boards go to chief executives of these organizations, giving them a formal say in workforce funding.
